title: rorca-cascade-prevention
specName: Cascade Prevention — In-Run Recovery for Failed Stories
brief: When a story fails or a worktree merge conflicts mid-run, the current engine immediately marks every transitive descendant `blocked_by` and ends the run with `failed` status — forcing the user to invoke `/api/pipeline/runs/:runId/retry` to recover. The descendant stories never had a chance to run, even though the underlying problem was often transient (flaky agent output, a merge conflict in a single file, an OpenCode socket hiccup). This spec redesigns in-run failure recovery so the run itself attempts recovery before declaring the cascade. The goal: a run that begins with N stories should end with the maximum possible stories passing, and only cascade-fail when a blocker has genuinely exhausted all recovery strategies.

contextUsed.direction: Rorca is a spec-driven orchestration platform. Every story runs in a dedicated git worktree; waves merge to the run-level worktree branch; the run-level worktree merges to main at run completion. The execution engine lives at backend/src/lib/execution-engine.ts and is spawned per-run by the pg-boss worker. The engine uses Kahn's algorithm (backend/src/lib/wave-compiler.ts) to compile stories into topologically-sorted waves. Each wave's stories run in parallel (bounded by config.parallelism); after the wave, passed worktrees merge via mergeWave() (LLM-assisted conflict resolution in autoResolveConflicts()); failed stories are collected into failedIds; computeBlockedStories() transitively marks every descendant with a failed ancestor as `blocked_by`.
contextUsed.currentBehavior: execution-engine.ts lines 3899-3920: at the START of each wave, stories whose dependsOn intersects failedIds are immediately marked skipped/failed with reason=blocked_by. Lines 4060-4083: after each wave, computeBlockedStories() performs a transitive closure and marks every reachable descendant blocked_by. There is no in-run retry of the blocker. There is no human-in-the-loop pause. There is no auto-rebase for merge conflicts. MAX_RETRIES=3 applies only within a single story execution (same wave, same moment) — once a story has exhausted its 3 attempts it is final for the run.
failureModes: merge_conflict: worktree branch merge produces conflicts LLM can't resolve (non-runtime files). Cascades all descendants.
max_retries: agent fails 3x with retryable errors (timeouts, transient tool failures). Cascades all descendants.
worktree_create_failed: git worktree add failed (disk full, permissions, ref exists). Cascades all descendants.
blocked_by (cascade): descendant auto-failed because ancestor failed. Not a real failure.
contextUsed.problem: In production run 20260316000215 of rorca-supabase-auth-rls (30 stories), MU-010 merge conflicted. This single failure cascaded blocked_by to 17 descendants including MU-011, MU-012, MU-013, MU-014, MU-015, MU-016, MU-021, MU-022, MU-023, MU-024, MU-025, MU-028, MU-029, MU-003, MU-030. The user had to invoke the retry endpoint to re-run all 17 stories in a NEW run — even though the merge conflict could have been re-attempted once within the same run.
architecturalConstraints: pg-boss worker spawns execution-engine.ts as a child process — the engine runs to completion and the worker updates pipeline_runs.status based on exit code.
Worktrees (.git/worktrees/<spec-slug>-<storyId>) are created BEFORE story execution and removed AFTER merge (success or failure). Re-running a story requires a fresh worktree.
The spec JSON's `passes` field is the durable source of truth for story completion — it survives crashes and is read by compileWaves() on next invocation.
story_results rows are per-run — a retry creates a new row with the same (run_id, story_id) and a separate status.
WAL events are append-only — story_failed with reason=blocked_by cannot be undone, only superseded by a later story_retried/story_passed event.
The run's own worktree (if autoWorktree=true) is merged to main ONLY on exit code 0 — cascade failures produce exit code 1 and the run-level worktree is left for manual merge.

userStories.title: Introduce failure classification with `transient` vs `terminal` categories
userStories.description: Today the engine has two failure categories: retryable (within-story, MAX_RETRIES=3) and non-retryable (invalid config). Neither captures the distinction between a failure that can be recovered by re-running the story AND a failure that cannot. Add a new classification dimension `recovery_class` with three values: `transient` (merge_conflict, worktree_create_failed_existing, worktree_create_failed_transient, auto_resolution_failed, agent_timeout, agent_rate_limit, agent_socket_error, agent_tool_transient), `terminal` (wrong_api_key, model_not_found, invalid_spec, agent_missing, gate_failure_after_max_retries, disk_full, permission_denied), and `policy_fail` (story's within-wave MAX_RETRIES=3 exhausted but the underlying failure reason was itself transient — operator policy dictates no further in-wave retry). Create `backend/src/lib/failure-classifier.ts` with `classifyFailure(reason: string, exitCode: number, stderr: string, context?: { retriesExhausted?: boolean }): FailureClassification`. The `reason` is a NORMALIZED enum (see acceptance criteria) — the classifier is pure on (reason, exitCode, stderr-substring-match, context), producing a deterministic (recoveryClass, category) pair. Critically: `reason='max_retries'` ALONE maps to recoveryClass='policy_fail', BUT callers that want recovery to proceed must pass the ORIGINAL reason (e.g. 'agent_timeout') instead of 'max_retries' when the within-wave retries exhausted a transient failure. This avoids the ambiguity of 'max_retries' meaning two different things. CP-008's dispatcher keys on (recoveryClass, reason) tuple, not reason alone.
acceptanceCriteria: backend/src/lib/failure-classifier.ts exports `classifyFailure(reason: FailureReason, exitCode: number, stderr: string, context?: { retriesExhausted?: boolean }): FailureClassification` where FailureReason is a TypeScript string-literal union enumerated in the exported const array `FAILURE_REASONS` (minimum: 'merge_conflict', 'auto_resolution_failed', 'agent_timeout', 'agent_rate_limit', 'agent_socket_error', 'agent_tool_transient', 'worktree_create_failed_existing', 'worktree_create_failed_transient', 'wrong_api_key', 'model_not_found', 'invalid_spec', 'agent_missing', 'gate_failure_after_max_retries', 'disk_full', 'permission_denied', 'max_retries', 'unknown').
FailureClassification = { recoveryClass: 'transient' | 'terminal' | 'policy_fail'; category: string; message: string; retryable: boolean }.
classifyFailure('merge_conflict', _, _) → recoveryClass='transient'.
classifyFailure('max_retries', _, _, {retriesExhausted:true}) → recoveryClass='policy_fail' (this is the explicit 'do not recover further' signal).
classifyFailure('agent_timeout', _, _) → recoveryClass='transient' regardless of whether within-wave retries were used.
classifyFailure('worktree_create_failed_existing', _, _) → recoveryClass='transient' (zombie branch from prior run).
classifyFailure('worktree_create_failed_transient', _, 'no space left on device') → recoveryClass='terminal' (disk full).
classifyFailure('auto_resolution_failed', _, _) → recoveryClass='transient'.
classifyFailure('wrong_api_key' | 'model_not_found' | 'agent_missing' | 'invalid_spec', _, _) → recoveryClass='terminal'.

Every call site of markStorySkipped() + emitWalEvent('story_failed') in execution-engine.ts uses the NORMALIZED reason enum (not 'max_retries' as a catch-all). Call sites that previously emitted `reason: 'max_retries'` now pass the underlying classified reason (e.g. 'agent_timeout') with context.retriesExhausted=true.
wal_events payload for story_failed includes both `reason` (normalized enum) and `recovery_class` fields.

Migration uses a FRESH timestamp assigned at implementation time (do NOT hardcode 20260422000000 — use the timestamp of the implementation PR date). Format: `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_story_results_failure_classification.sql`. Migration adds `failure_reason TEXT NULL` and `recovery_class TEXT NULL CHECK (recovery_class IS NULL OR recovery_class IN ('transient','terminal','policy_fail'))`.

Unit test at backend/src/lib/__tests__/failure-classifier.test.ts covers at MINIMUM the 17 FAILURE_REASONS enum values plus 3 edge cases (unknown reason → terminal, empty stderr, exitCode=0 with retryable reason is a no-op).

Backward compatibility: old wal_events and story_results rows without `recovery_class` remain readable (reader code treats missing as 'terminal' to prevent accidental recovery of historical failures).
`FAILURE_REASONS` enum is re-exported from execution-engine.ts so call sites can import it type-safely.

userStories.title: Replace `failedIds: Set<string>` with `failureRegistry: Map<storyId, FailureRecord>`
userStories.description: The cascade logic at execution-engine.ts line 3879 uses `failedIds: Set<string>` — a boolean set with no metadata. To drive intelligent recovery we need richer information per failure: when it failed, what wave, what the classification was, how many recovery attempts have been made, whether it's currently being recovered, and its worktree state. Replace the Set with a Map<string, FailureRecord> where FailureRecord contains: `{ storyId, waveIndex, failedAt: number, reason: string, recoveryClass, recoveryAttempts: number, lastRecoveryAt: number | null, recoveryInFlight: boolean, conflictingFiles?: string[], stderrTail?: string }`. All reads (`failedIds.has(dep)`, `failedIds.add(id)`) must be replaced with Map methods. Add helper functions `markStoryFailed(registry, record)`, `isStoryFailed(registry, id)`, `getFailureRecord(registry, id)`. Preserve the semantic that passed stories eventually removed from the registry (when a recovery succeeds). This is the foundational data-structure change — every subsequent story builds on this registry.
acceptanceCriteria: execution-engine.ts declares `const failureRegistry = new Map<string, FailureRecord>()` replacing the previous `failedIds: Set<string>`.
FailureRecord interface is defined and exported from execution-engine.ts (or a new backend/src/lib/failure-registry.ts).
Every `failedIds.add(id)` is replaced with `markStoryFailed(failureRegistry, { ... })`.
Every `failedIds.has(dep)` is replaced with `isStoryFailed(failureRegistry, dep)`.
The computeBlockedStories() function accepts a Map (or Set extracted from it for compatibility) and produces the same blocked transitively-closed map.
A passed recovery removes the entry from the registry (verified in CP-007).
Unit test covers: (a) marking a story failed creates a record with waveIndex, (b) checking a non-failed story returns false, (c) removing a record makes it non-failed.
tsc --noEmit passes across backend/.

Existing wave execution path (single-story wave, multi-story wave, cascade) still produces the same story_results rows and WAL events as before this refactor — verified by an integration test that runs a 3-story spec with 1 intentional failure and asserts the same blocked_by cascade occurs (behavior unchanged until CP-003+).

userStories.title: Defer blocked_by marking to end-of-wave rather than start-of-wave
userStories.description: Currently the engine scans each wave's stories at the START (lines 3889-3923) and immediately marks any story with a failed dep as `blocked_by` and skips it. This is the root of the cascade problem: once MU-010 failed in wave 2, every dependent in wave 3 was marked blocked_by BEFORE wave 3 even started — no opportunity for MU-010 to recover. Change the flow: at the start of each wave, stories with failed deps are NOT marked blocked_by. Instead they are held in a `deferredStories` list. The wave executes only the executable stories (all deps either passed or not in failureRegistry). AFTER the wave completes and its merge is done, attempt recovery on blockers (CP-005). Only at end-of-wave — after recovery attempts — do we run computeBlockedStories() and emit blocked_by events for the transitive closure that remains. This preserves the existing cascade semantics as a LAST RESORT. DEFINITIONS: 'transitively depends on' means the full recursive closure (a story X transitively depends on Y if X's dependsOn includes Y OR any of X's dependencies transitively depends on Y). This is computed via BFS from the failureRegistry entries. SERIALIZATION CONTRACT: the recovery phase for wave N MUST COMPLETE before wave N+1 begins. Wave N+1's compilation reads the updated passes state AFTER wave N's recovery finishes. This is enforced by awaiting `attemptBlockerRecovery()` synchronously in the wave loop. No parallelism between recovery and the next wave (would introduce race conditions on cwd HEAD).
acceptanceCriteria: execution-engine.ts wave loop no longer marks `blocked_by` at the TOP of the wave (lines 3899-3920 pre-wave scan logic is removed; replaced with partition into executable + deferred).

Partition logic: for each story in wave, if `all(dep => !isStoryFailed(failureRegistry, dep))` then executable, else deferred. 'Deferred' means waiting for recovery — does NOT mark the story as failed yet.
Deferred stories are tracked in a wave-local `deferredStories: UserStory[]` — NOT added to failureRegistry (they haven't actually failed).

The wave's `executableStories` list only contains stories whose deps are all passed (or unknown/excluded — compiled waves already exclude passed stories from subsequent waves, so 'unknown' should not arise).

After the wave's merge completes (lines 3986-4056 mechanics unchanged), the engine calls `attemptBlockerRecovery(...)` (implemented in CP-005) and AWAITS its completion synchronously. The next wave's iteration MUST NOT begin until this promise resolves.

After recovery, computeBlockedStories() is invoked with the UPDATED failureRegistry (blockers that recovered have been removed) to compute the REMAINING transitive closure, and emits blocked_by events ONLY for stories still blocked.

If a story was deferred but its blocking ancestor recovered, the story is NOT marked blocked_by — it returns to the pool and becomes executable in the wave where its deps resolve (typically the current wave, if re-eligible).

RE-EXECUTION OF DEFERRED STORIES: if recovery unblocked a story that was deferred in the CURRENT wave, the engine attempts to execute it IN THE CURRENT WAVE (a second mini-wave after recovery) rather than waiting until wave N+1. This is the 'deferred-retry pass' — implementation: after recovery, re-run the partition, any newly-executable stories from deferredStories are added to an in-wave retry batch and executed (bounded by config.parallelism).
A `cascade_deferred` WAL event is emitted per deferred story `{ run_id, story_id, deferred_due_to: string[], wave_index, deferred_at: ISO }`.
A `cascade_deferred_executed` WAL event is emitted for each deferred story that becomes executable post-recovery `{ run_id, story_id, wave_index, recovery_unblocked_by: string[] }`.
UI semantics (referenced by CP-013 dashboard): deferred stories show as 'awaiting ancestor recovery' (distinct from 'queued' and 'running') in the Run View.

Integration test 1 (single-level dep): 4-story spec where story A fails once then succeeds on recovery, B deps on A, C deps on B, D independent — D runs in its wave, B and C are deferred, A recovers, B runs (same wave as recovery), C runs (next wave), all four pass.
Integration test 2 (deep chain): 10-story chain A→B→...→J, A fails twice then succeeds on 3rd attempt (cap hit). All 10 pass, with cascade_deferred events for B–J accumulated across waves.

Integration test 3 (recovery-failure cascade): A fails, 2 recovery attempts exhaust. B, C (deps on A) are deferred then cascaded blocked_by. D (independent) passes. Final run status = partial_failure.

Integration test 4 (serialization check): instrument attemptBlockerRecovery to emit a probe event at start/end; verify wave N+1's first executeStory call has a timestamp strictly after wave N's recovery-end probe.
Existing test coverage (retry.test.ts, retry-merge.test.ts) continues to pass — this change is forward-compatible since recovery is gated behind cascadePrevention=true (CP-014).

userStories.title: Persist a global recovery-attempts counter per story per run
userStories.description: Runaway recovery loops are the biggest risk: a transient-classified failure could recover-fail-recover-fail indefinitely, burning tokens and wall-clock. Each story needs a persistent recovery-attempts counter visible both to the engine and to the DB so operators can audit it. Add a migration adding columns `recovery_attempts INTEGER DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL` and `max_recovery_attempts INTEGER DEFAULT 2 NOT NULL` to `story_results`. Emit events when incrementing. Enforce a hard ceiling of 2 recovery attempts per story per run (configurable per-story via `story.maxRecoveryAttempts` in spec JSON; default 2 if unset). The ceiling is additive to the existing MAX_RETRIES=3 within-story budget: 3 attempts-per-execution × (1 initial + 2 recoveries) = up to 9 agent invocations per story per run, worst case. Log this budget clearly at run start so operators understand the cost model.
acceptanceCriteria: Migration uses a FRESH timestamp at implementation time (format YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_story_results_recovery_counter.sql). Adds `recovery_attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` and `max_recovery_attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 2` to story_results.
FailureRecord (CP-002) carries `recoveryAttempts: number` and `maxRecoveryAttempts: number` mirroring DB state.
Each recovery attempt increments the counter via UPDATE story_results SET recovery_attempts = recovery_attempts + 1 WHERE run_id = $1 AND story_id = $2.
Default max_recovery_attempts = 2 (configurable via `storyMaxRecoveryAttempts` in spec top-level JSON or per-story `maxRecoveryAttempts`).
When recovery_attempts >= max_recovery_attempts, the recovery subsystem (CP-005, CP-006) refuses to attempt and the cascade proceeds.
At run_started, emit a log line like 'Recovery budget: ≤2 recovery attempts per story, ≤3 retries per attempt = ≤9 agent invocations/story worst case'.
wal_events.story_recovery_attempted event carries `attempt: number, budget: number` in payload.
Integration test: a story fails, attempts recovery twice, both fail, on the third attempt the engine refuses and emits blocked_by cascade for descendants. Story_results row has recovery_attempts=2.
Zero migration collisions — timestamp-format filename sorts after existing migrations.

userStories.title: Implement `attemptBlockerRecovery()` — the core in-wave recovery orchestrator
userStories.description: This is the heart of the cascade-prevention system. After each wave completes and its merge is done, invoke a new `attemptBlockerRecovery(...)` function. ELIGIBILITY (precise): an eligible blocker is a FailureRecord where ALL of: (a) recoveryClass === 'transient'; (b) recoveryAttempts < maxRecoveryAttempts; (c) recoveryInFlight === false; (d) at least one story in `deferredStories` transitively depends on this blocker (BFS through dependsOn edges). ORDERING: blockers are processed in a deterministic order — alphabetical by storyId — so reproducibility is preserved across runs. BOUNDED PARALLELISM: recovery tasks run via `runWithBoundedConcurrency(tasks, recoveryCap)` where `recoveryCap = Math.max(1, Math.floor(config.parallelism / 3))`. For `config.parallelism=1`, recoveryCap=1 (sequential). For `config.parallelism=10`, recoveryCap=3. IDEMPOTENCY: each recovery task sets `failureRecord.recoveryInFlight=true` at start AND atomically increments `story_results.recovery_attempts` via `UPDATE story_results SET recovery_attempts = recovery_attempts + 1 WHERE run_id=$1 AND story_id=$2 RETURNING recovery_attempts`. If the engine crashes mid-recovery, the DB shows the increment but no terminal recovery event — CP-018 reconciliation handles this. PARTIAL RECOVERY SUCCESS: if some blockers recover and others fail, we proceed with the partial wins — the function returns lists of recovered/stillFailed. The caller (CP-003 wave loop) uses these lists to update spec JSON and emit events.
acceptanceCriteria: New file backend/src/lib/blocker-recovery.ts exports `async function attemptBlockerRecovery(params: { failureRegistry: Map<string, FailureRecord>; deferredStories: UserStory[]; allStories: UserStory[]; config: EngineConfig; mode: ExecutionMode; playbook: PlaybookContext; logDir: string; workspaceId: string | null; retryCounts: Map<string, number>; personaRegistry: PersonaRegistry; waveIndex: number; specForBrowserMcp: SpecJson }): Promise<RecoveryWaveResult>` where `RecoveryWaveResult = { recovered: string[]; stillFailed: string[]; noRecoveryNeeded: string[]; circuitOpenedSkipped: boolean }`.

Eligibility check (all must hold): (a) record.recoveryClass === 'transient', (b) record.recoveryAttempts < record.maxRecoveryAttempts, (c) record.recoveryInFlight === false, (d) at least one story in deferredStories has failureRecord.storyId in its transitive-dependsOn closure. The closure is computed via BFS on the dependsOn graph of deferredStories.
Deterministic ordering: eligible blockers are processed alphabetically by storyId — reproducibility across runs.
Concurrency: `runWithBoundedConcurrency(tasks, Math.max(1, Math.floor(config.parallelism / 3)))`. Recovery NEVER monopolizes the engine.

Atomicity: each recovery task starts with `record.recoveryInFlight = true` and executes an atomic SQL increment `UPDATE story_results SET recovery_attempts = recovery_attempts + 1, updated_at = NOW() WHERE run_id=$1 AND story_id=$2 RETURNING recovery_attempts`. This runs BEFORE the strategy function so the DB reflects in-flight state even on crash.

Each recovery task calls `dispatchRecovery(record, context)` (CP-008). On success: the task marks passes in spec JSON via `markStoryPassed(config.jsonPath, storyId)` (critical — this resets the passes:false written during original failure per CP-006 issue #2), removes the record from failureRegistry, emits `story_passed` WAL event with `{ run_id, story_id, via: 'recovery', recovery_attempt: N, strategy, duration_ms }`, and posts /api/pipeline/story-result with status='pass' and via='recovery'.

On strategy failure: the task sets `record.recoveryInFlight = false`, keeps the record in the registry, emits `story_recovery_failed` WAL event with `{ run_id, story_id, reason, strategy, attempt: N, duration_ms }`. If attempts now equals maxRecoveryAttempts, additionally emit a `story_recovery_exhausted` event (distinct signal for downstream UI/analytics).
Summary log at function end: `[recovery] wave ${N}: eligible=${X}, recovered=${Y}, still-failed=${Z}, skipped-no-dependents=${W}, skipped-max-attempts=${V}`.
Safe-invocation: with empty deferredStories list, function returns `{ recovered: [], stillFailed: [], noRecoveryNeeded: [], circuitOpenedSkipped: false }` immediately with no WAL events or DB writes.

Circuit-breaker hook: CP-010's circuit decision is consulted BEFORE enumerating eligible blockers — if circuit is open, function emits `recovery_circuit_opened` (per CP-010) and returns `{ recovered: [], stillFailed: [], noRecoveryNeeded: [], circuitOpenedSkipped: true }`.

Integration test 1 (merge_conflict recovery): blocker fails with merge_conflict, one deferred descendant. Recovery succeeds via CP-006 strategy. recovered=[blockerId], stillFailed=[], descendant proceeds to execute.
Integration test 2 (exhaust cap): blocker fails twice (recovery_attempts=1→2), third call is blocked by eligibility check (attempts >= maxRecoveryAttempts). Descendant cascades blocked_by.

Integration test 3 (terminal blocker): blocker fails with wrong_api_key (terminal). Eligibility check excludes it. Function returns noRecoveryNeeded=[] (terminal blockers aren't included in any category from this function's perspective — they're handled by the cascade directly).
Integration test 4 (eligibility — no dependents): blocker fails, but its only dependent was excluded in the spec. Function skips this blocker (noRecoveryNeeded), does NOT waste a recovery attempt.

Integration test 5 (partial recovery): wave has 3 blockers. Blocker A recovers, B fails strategy, C is ineligible. recovered=[A], stillFailed=[B], noRecoveryNeeded=[C]. A's descendants unblock; B's and C's cascade.
Unit test: empty deferredStories → immediate return, no mutations.
Unit test: ordering determinism — 3 eligible blockers (Z-001, A-001, M-001) — verify processing order is alphabetical (A-001, M-001, Z-001).

userStories.title: Merge-conflict recovery: auto-rebase against updated base + retry conflict resolution
userStories.description: The most common `transient` failure is merge_conflict — a story's worktree can't cleanly merge because a concurrent wave-merge modified overlapping files. Today this immediately fails (execution-engine.ts line 3990-4000 and 4026-4054). Recovery strategy: (1) identify the story's worktree branch (it still exists because mergeWave() only removes successfully-merged worktrees; failed-merge worktrees are preserved per line 4052-4053 — `Failed worktree branches preserved for inspection.`); (2) compute the rebase target as the CURRENT HEAD of the run-level cwd (which may be main, or the auto-worktree branch `feat/<slug>-<ts>` if autoWorktree=true) — use `git -C <cwd> rev-parse HEAD` to get a concrete SHA, NOT a branch name (avoids races with concurrent writers); (3) cd into the story worktree, ensure working tree is clean via `git -C <worktreePath> status --porcelain` (if dirty, commit any uncommitted changes as `chore: pre-rebase runtime files` — same pattern as mergeStoryWorktree line 2120-2128); (4) run `git -C <worktreePath> rebase <target-sha>`; (5) if rebase introduces conflicts, invoke `autoResolveConflicts()` (existing, move to shared module) per conflicting file, then `git rebase --continue`; (6) if rebase succeeds, re-invoke `mergeStoryWorktree(cwd, worktree)` which merges the rebased branch into cwd; (7) if any step fails, the function returns { success: false, reason, conflictingFiles }, preserves the worktree for inspection, and increments recovery_attempts; (8) CRITICAL: on successful recovery, the caller (CP-005) MUST call `markStoryPassed(config.jsonPath, storyId)` to RESET the spec JSON `passes:false` that was written by `markStoryMergeFailed()` at line 3994/4034 during the original failure. Without this reset, the final `finalSpec = JSON.parse(...)` read at line 4089 will still show passes=false and the run exit code logic will disagree with story_results. Note: NO `git fetch` is needed — all refs are local (main, autoWorktree branch, story worktree branches) and worktrees share the parent repo's .git/refs directory.
acceptanceCriteria: New function `recoverMergeConflict(storyId: string, worktree: StoryWorktree, cwd: string, logDir: string): Promise<{ success: boolean; reason?: string; conflictingFiles?: string[]; targetSha: string }>` in backend/src/lib/blocker-recovery.ts.

The function computes the rebase target by running `git -C <cwd> rev-parse HEAD` and using the returned SHA as a concrete immutable target (not a branch name — avoids races with concurrent wave merges happening in parallel).
The function runs `git -C <worktreePath> status --porcelain` first; if non-empty, runs `git add -A && git commit -m 'chore: pre-rebase runtime files' --allow-empty` to ensure clean working tree.
The function runs `git -C <worktreePath> rebase <target-sha>` (NO `git fetch` — refs are local).

On rebase conflict, autoResolveConflicts() is invoked (existing function at execution-engine.ts line 2186; this story does NOT move it, it's imported directly from the existing location to minimize churn).
After autoResolveConflicts succeeds, the function runs `git -C <worktreePath> -c core.editor=true rebase --continue` with a 30s timeout.
The function then calls `mergeStoryWorktree(cwd, worktree)` (existing function line 2115) to merge the rebased branch into cwd.

On success, the function returns `{ success: true, targetSha }` and the CALLER (CP-005) is responsible for calling `markStoryPassed(config.jsonPath, storyId)` AND `removeStoryWorktree(cwd, worktree)` — recoverMergeConflict does NOT mutate spec JSON or remove the worktree itself (separation of concerns).

On failure (rebase cannot proceed, LLM resolution fails, second merge fails, timeout), the function runs `git -C <worktreePath> rebase --abort` to restore the worktree to its pre-rebase state, and returns `{ success: false, reason: string, conflictingFiles: string[], targetSha }`.

The function emits `merge_recovery_attempted` WAL event with `{ run_id, story_id, target_sha }` BEFORE the rebase and `merge_recovery_succeeded` or `merge_recovery_failed` with `{ run_id, story_id, target_sha, duration_ms, conflicting_files? }` at the end.

Integration test: 2 stories in wave N+1 both modify backend/src/routes/users.ts. Story X merges cleanly first; story Y merge-conflicts. Recovery rebases Y onto HEAD (which now includes X's commits), LLM resolves the conflict, Y merges successfully. Both stories pass. Final spec JSON shows passes=true for both.

Integration test: merge recovery fails because conflicts include a file the LLM cannot resolve (stub test injects invalid JSON into LLM response). Function returns success:false. Worktree remains at pre-rebase state. recovery_attempts incremented.

Integration test: concurrent wave-merge happening in parallel — test seeds a scenario where HEAD moves between rev-parse and rebase start. Verify rebase uses the captured SHA (doesn't chase a moving target).
Safety: the function operates inside the story's worktree via `git -C <worktreePath>`, not cwd — failed recovery cannot corrupt cwd's HEAD.
Logs include: the target-SHA, the exact git commands run, stderr tails, and autoResolveConflicts per-file outcomes.

Mixed-conflict safety: autoResolveConflicts already distinguishes tracking files (fast-path --theirs) from real code (LLM resolution, per execution-engine.ts lines 2212-2297). Recovery does NOT override this behavior — a mixed runtime+code conflict uses the existing per-file resolution (tracking files auto-resolved, code files LLM-resolved). If ANY code-file LLM resolution returns null, the overall recovery is treated as failed and the rebase is aborted.

autoWorktree=false handling: when autoWorktree=false, cwd IS the main workspace directory. The rebase target SHA captured via `git -C <cwd> rev-parse HEAD` is the main branch HEAD. This works — the recovery target is whatever the run is actually committing against. No special-casing needed.

userStories.title: Agent-failure recovery: fresh worktree + escalated prompt
userStories.description: The second recovery strategy is for stories that failed via a transient agent error (timeout, opencode socket error, rate limit, tool transient) where within-wave MAX_RETRIES=3 exhausted. Strategy: (1) the original worktree is long gone (removeStoryWorktree was called after failure per line 4058); (2) create a NEW worktree with a distinct branch name (see acceptance criteria for naming); (3) the recovery worktree branches off the CURRENT HEAD of cwd — which may have advanced since the original failure because subsequent waves merged their stories. This means recovery sees those merged commits as its starting state, which is intentional and correct; (4) re-execute the story through `executeStory()` with three augmentations: (a) the shared retryCounts Map has its entry for this storyId deleted (`retryCounts.delete(storyId)`) so executeStory's internal MAX_RETRIES counter starts fresh (the budget model: 3 within-wave retries × up to 2 recoveries = max 9 agent invocations per story per run, worst case); (b) `buildPrompt()` is called with an additional injected context block `[RECOVERY CONTEXT: ...]` explaining the prior failure's stderrTail (last 2KB) and instructing the agent to try a different approach; (c) if CP-011 model-escalation is enabled, the model tier is bumped one level (OpenCode only; no-op for Claude/Codex subscription agents); (5) on success, the NEW worktree is merged via `mergeStoryWorktree(cwd, recoveryWorktree)` (CP-006 auto-rebase kicks in if the merge conflicts); (6) on failure, the recovery worktree is cleaned up, recovery_attempts is incremented. Because `executeStory()` internally consults `retryCounts.get(storyId)` and `MAX_RETRIES=3` to decide when to return 'failed', the delete is sufficient to grant a fresh within-wave budget.
acceptanceCriteria: New function `recoverAgentFailure(params: { storyId: string; originalStory: UserStory; cwd: string; config: EngineConfig; mode: ExecutionMode; playbook: PlaybookContext; logDir: string; workspaceId: string | null; stories: UserStory[]; retryCounts: Map<string, number>; attemptNumber: number; originalStderrTail: string; personaRegistry: PersonaRegistry; waveIndex: number; specForBrowserMcp: SpecJson }): Promise<{ success: boolean; reason?: string }>` in backend/src/lib/blocker-recovery.ts.

PREREQUISITE: `createStoryWorktree()` (currently at execution-engine.ts ~line 2056) is modified to accept an optional fourth argument: `opts?: { branchSuffix?: string; collisionBehavior?: 'uuid' | 'fail' }`. When `branchSuffix` is provided, the branch name becomes `feat/${specSlug}-${storyId}-${branchSuffix}` (no timestamp). When `collisionBehavior='uuid'`, on collision with an existing branch, the function appends a random 8-hex-char suffix and retries (max 3 attempts).
recoverAgentFailure() calls `createStoryWorktree(cwd, specSlug, storyId, { branchSuffix: `recovery-${attemptNumber}`, collisionBehavior: 'uuid' })`.
recoverAgentFailure() calls `retryCounts.delete(storyId)` BEFORE invoking executeStory() to reset the within-wave retry budget.

recoverAgentFailure() passes an AUGMENTED story to executeStory: a shallow clone of originalStory with `story.description = originalStory.description + '\n\n[RECOVERY CONTEXT: This story previously failed (attempt #${attemptNumber-1}) with error tail: "${originalStderrTail.slice(-2000)}". The prior worktree and changes have been discarded. Please analyze the failure and try a different approach.]'`. The original story object is NOT mutated.
executeStory() is invoked with waveIndex encoded as `waveIndex * 1000 + attemptNumber` (uniqueness: 3 digits of recovery attempt per wave).

On success (executeStory returns 'passed'): the function returns `{ success: true }`. The CALLER (CP-005) is responsible for removing the worktree via removeStoryWorktree(), marking the story passed via markStoryPassed(), and emitting the story_passed WAL event.
On failure (executeStory returns 'failed'): the function removes the recovery worktree, returns `{ success: false, reason: 'agent_recovery_failed' }`. The CALLER increments recovery_attempts.

Branch name collision: if the collision retries exhaust (3 attempts), recoverAgentFailure returns `{ success: false, reason: 'worktree_name_collision' }` and the caller treats this as a recovery failure (it counts toward recovery_attempts).
The function logs: (a) the original stderrTail being injected, (b) the new branch name, (c) the MAX_RETRIES budget status, (d) the model used (bumped or not).

userStories.title: Recovery strategy dispatcher: routes FailureRecord to the right recovery function
userStories.description: Consolidate CP-006, CP-007, CP-009 behind a single dispatcher so future recovery strategies can be added without changing the orchestrator. Create `dispatchRecovery(failureRecord: FailureRecord, context: RecoveryContext): Promise<RecoveryOutcome>` which keys on the TUPLE `(recoveryClass, reason)` — NOT reason alone. This disambiguates cases where the same reason string could map to different strategies (e.g. worktree_create_failed with 'already exists' → CP-009 cleanup+retry, vs worktree_create_failed with terminal stderr → no strategy). Mapping table is exhaustive and enumerated in acceptance criteria. For any unmapped (transient, <unknown-reason>) tuple, the dispatcher logs a warning, emits a `recovery_no_strategy` WAL event, and returns a no-strategy outcome — this is the safe default. For `recoveryClass='terminal'`, the dispatcher short-circuits without calling any strategy. For `recoveryClass='policy_fail'`, the dispatcher also short-circuits (operator policy says no further recovery).
acceptanceCriteria: Function `dispatchRecovery(failureRecord: FailureRecord, context: RecoveryContext): Promise<RecoveryOutcome>` exported from backend/src/lib/blocker-recovery.ts.

RecoveryOutcome = { success: boolean; reason?: string; strategy: RecoveryStrategy; durationMs: number }. RecoveryStrategy = 'merge_rebase' | 'agent_fresh_worktree' | 'worktree_cleanup_retry' | 'llm_resolve_replay' | 'no_strategy'.

Dispatcher keys on the TUPLE `(recoveryClass, reason)` via a switch/dispatch table. Exhaustive mapping: (transient, merge_conflict)→merge_rebase; (transient, auto_resolution_failed)→llm_resolve_replay (re-invoke autoResolveConflicts with a different prompt); (transient, agent_timeout)→agent_fresh_worktree; (transient, agent_rate_limit)→agent_fresh_worktree (with exponential backoff delay before spawning); (transient, agent_socket_error)→agent_fresh_worktree; (transient, agent_tool_transient)→agent_fresh_worktree; (transient, worktree_create_failed_existing)→worktree_cleanup_retry; (transient, worktree_create_failed_transient)→agent_fresh_worktree; (transient, *any other transient reason*)→no_strategy with warning log; (terminal, *)→no_strategy (short-circuit); (policy_fail, *)→no_strategy (short-circuit).
Unmapped transient returns `{ success: false, reason: 'no_strategy_for_reason', strategy: 'no_strategy', durationMs }` and emits a `recovery_no_strategy` WAL event.
Terminal short-circuit returns `{ success: false, reason: 'terminal_non_recoverable', strategy: 'no_strategy', durationMs }` WITHOUT emitting no_strategy WAL (terminal is expected, not noteworthy).
Policy-fail short-circuit returns `{ success: false, reason: 'policy_fail_no_further_recovery', strategy: 'no_strategy', durationMs }`.
Dispatcher records `durationMs` using performance.now() at entry and exit — includes dispatch routing overhead plus strategy function wall-clock.
Dispatcher emits a `recovery_dispatch` WAL event BEFORE invoking the strategy function with `{ run_id, story_id, reason, recovery_class, strategy, attempt_number }`.
No shared mutable state in the dispatcher itself — all state mutation happens in the invoked strategy functions.
Unit test: each of the 11+ tuple mappings exercised explicitly (minimum 11 tests — one per mapping row).
Unit test: a transient tuple with reason='foo_unknown' correctly routes to no_strategy with a warn log.
Unit test: (terminal, wrong_api_key) short-circuits without calling any recovery function (mock verifies no invocation).

The exact mapping table is defined as a top-of-file constant `const RECOVERY_STRATEGY_MAP: Record<\`${RecoveryClass}:${FailureReason}\`, RecoveryStrategy>` so both humans and future AI implementers see it at a glance.

userStories.title: Worktree-create-failed recovery: cleanup + retry with UUID suffix
userStories.description: When a worktree creation fails with `fatal: 'feat/...' is already checked out at` or `invalid reference`, today the engine immediately adds the story to failedIds (execution-engine.ts lines 3937-3952). This is fully transient — a zombie worktree from a prior interrupted run. Recovery: (1) detect the orphaned worktree/branch via `git worktree list --porcelain` and `git branch -a`; (2) remove the orphan: `git worktree remove --force <path>` and `git branch -D <branch>`; (3) retry worktree creation with a UUID-suffixed branch name `feat/<slug>-<storyId>-<uuid8>` to guarantee uniqueness. This recovery fires at worktree-creation time (before execution) and is distinct from post-execution recovery — it belongs in the worktree-creation code path but uses the same FailureRecord infrastructure for observability.
acceptanceCriteria: New function `cleanupOrphanedWorktree(cwd, branchPrefix)` in backend/src/lib/worktree-recovery.ts that scans git worktree list and removes any matching prefix.

createStoryWorktree() gains an optional `{ retryOnConflict: boolean }` param; when true, on error stderr contains 'already checked out' or 'already exists', the function calls cleanupOrphanedWorktree() and retries creation with a UUID-suffixed branch.
The dispatcher (CP-008) routes `worktree_create_failed` with 'already exists' stderr to this recovery path.
A `worktree_cleanup_attempted` WAL event is emitted with { storyId, orphanedBranch, uuidSuffix }.
If cleanup succeeds and re-creation succeeds, the story proceeds through normal execution (CP-007 is invoked if the story itself also needs re-execution).
If cleanup fails (permissions, filesystem error), the failure is marked terminal (CP-001 classification) and no further recovery is attempted.
Integration test: simulate an orphaned worktree by creating `feat/testspec-S1` ahead of the run; recovery detects it, removes it, creates feat/testspec-S1-<uuid>, story executes successfully.
Safety: only branches matching feat/<spec-slug>-* prefix are candidates for cleanup — never touches user feature branches.

userStories.title: Circuit breaker: halt recovery if >50% of wave's stories need recovery
userStories.description: If a wave has 10 stories and 6 of them need recovery, something systemic is wrong — agent is degraded, API is having an outage, the spec has a bad instruction, etc. Recovering them individually would be wasteful and likely to fail anyway. Implement a circuit breaker: if at the end of wave N, more than THRESHOLD of wave N's EXECUTED stories failed with recoveryClass='transient', DO NOT attempt recovery — emit `recovery_circuit_opened`, log loudly, and cascade. DEFINITIONS (critical — both numerator and denominator are precise): the DENOMINATOR is `executedStories` = stories for which the engine invoked `executeStory()` (i.e. worktree was created AND agent subprocess was spawned — even if the agent failed). Stories that never executed (worktree_create_failed — never got past creation) are EXCLUDED from the denominator entirely; they go into the separate `worktreeCreationFailures` count and are handled independently. Stories deferred via CP-003 (blocked_by but not yet cascaded) are NOT in the denominator. The NUMERATOR is `transientRecoveryCandidates` = failures with recoveryClass='transient' that are eligible for recovery (have a transitive descendant still waiting). Terminal failures don't count; policy_fail doesn't count. This means a wave where all 10 workstrees fail to create (disk full) does NOT open the circuit (executedStories=0, divide-by-zero guard returns false), but the engine logs an error and still skips recovery (nothing to recover). Threshold is configurable via spec JSON top-level `recoveryCircuitThreshold: number` (0.0–1.0, default 0.5).
acceptanceCriteria: After each wave completes and before calling attemptBlockerRecovery, the engine calculates `circuit.executedStories = stories in wave that had createStoryWorktree return non-null AND executeStory was invoked`.
The engine calculates `circuit.transientRecoveryCandidates = failures in wave with failureRecord.recoveryClass === 'transient' AND at least one transitive deferred descendant`.

If `circuit.executedStories === 0`, circuit is treated as CLOSED (no divide-by-zero), but the engine logs `[recovery] Wave N: no stories executed — skipping recovery (typically worktree creation failed for all).` and moves on.
If `circuit.executedStories > 0`: `failureRate = circuit.transientRecoveryCandidates.length / circuit.executedStories.length`. If `failureRate > recoveryCircuitThreshold`, circuit OPENS.

When circuit opens: emit `recovery_circuit_opened` WAL event with `{ run_id, wave_index, failure_rate, threshold, executed_count, transient_failure_count, failed_stories: string[] }`. Log: `[recovery] Circuit OPEN for wave N — ${transientFailureCount}/${executedCount} transient failures (${(failureRate*100).toFixed(1)}%) exceeds threshold ${(threshold*100).toFixed(1)}%. Skipping recovery. Root cause likely systemic.`
computeBlockedStories() still runs AFTER the circuit decision (cascade proceeds); recovery is the thing that's skipped.
The circuit decision is recorded per-wave; wave N+1's decision is independent (each wave computes its own failureRate).

Special threshold values: `0` means recovery is DISABLED (circuit always open); `1.01` (or any value >1) means recovery is ALWAYS attempted (circuit never opens); `1.0` means circuit opens only when 100% of executed stories failed transiently (effectively never opens, since a 100% failure rate means nothing succeeded to trigger end-of-wave); default `0.5` means strictly more than half.
Unit test 1 (normal open): wave with 10 executed stories, 6 transient failures with eligible descendants, threshold 0.5 → circuit opens.
Unit test 2 (normal closed): wave with 10 executed, 4 transient failures, threshold 0.5 → closed; recovery attempted.
Unit test 3 (terminals don't count): wave with 10 executed, 6 failures of which 3 are terminal and 3 transient, threshold 0.5 → numerator=3, denominator=10, rate=0.3, closed.

Unit test 4 (divide-by-zero safety): wave with 0 executed stories (all worktree_create_failed), threshold 0.5 → closed (circuit cannot open on empty denominator); warning log fires; recovery skipped because nothing to recover.

Unit test 5 (descendant gating): wave with 10 executed, 6 transient failures but 4 of them have NO deferred descendants (their downstream stories passed or are excluded). Numerator=2, denominator=10, rate=0.2, closed.
Unit test 6 (exact boundary): 5/10 = 0.5 with threshold 0.5 → 'strictly more than' means circuit remains CLOSED (the 50% case is allowed to recover).

userStories.title: Recovery-with-escalation: optional model-tier bump on agent-failure recovery
userStories.description: When recoverAgentFailure() runs, the obvious improvement over 'same model, new worktree, different prompt' is to escalate the model tier. Rorca supports multiple providers — Anthropic (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), OpenAI (mini/standard/flagship), Google (Flash/Pro), OpenRouter (auto), Ollama (user-specified). Define an escalation table per provider. Add `recoveryModelEscalation: boolean` toggle to spec JSON (default false — deterministic behavior for testing) and workspace-level default. For subscription agents (claude, codex), escalation is a no-op on model (no model choice) — recovery still appends the context block. ESCALATION RULES: (1) if original model is the provider's MAX tier already, stay at max (no further escalation); (2) for OpenRouter (model='openrouter/auto'), escalation is a no-op (router chooses); (3) for Ollama local models, no escalation — operator has full control; (4) escalation bumps ONE tier per recovery attempt cumulatively (if recovery 1 goes Sonnet→Opus, recovery 2 stays at Opus).

userStories.title: HITL pause option: user can intervene before cascade
userStories.description: Some failures are operator-decidable — the agent can't recover but a human tweak (API schema changed, env var missing, etc.) could unstick it. Add `hitlPauseOnFailure: 'none' | 'terminal-only' | 'all-transient' | 'after-max-recovery'` (default 'after-max-recovery'). CRITICAL DESIGN DECISIONS: (1) PAUSE IS PER-WAVE, NOT PER-FAILURE. If a wave ends with 4 blockers eligible for HITL, the engine pauses ONCE with all 4 in the payload. The operator gets one pause per wave with aggregated context. (2) PAUSE SEMANTICS: the engine process stays ALIVE (no SIGSTOP/SIGCONT). It enters an in-process poll loop (setInterval every 3s) that checks for flag files. This is intentionally different from the legacy `/context` SIGCONT path — cascade-prevention HITL uses the poll-loop exclusively. The legacy `/context` endpoint's SIGCONT send is now a no-op when pipeline_runs.status='paused' with paused_mode='hitl_cascade_prevention' (detected via a new column). (3) RESUME ACTIONS: three endpoints — `/context` (existing, writes context file, engine picks it up and re-enters recovery with the context appended), `/resume` (existing, writes resume flag, engine cascades the current blockers without further recovery attempts), `/skip-story` (NEW, writes per-story skip flag, engine marks that story as policy_fail and proceeds to cascade its subtree without cascading siblings). Timeout: `hitlPauseTimeoutMinutes` (default 30, bounds 1–1440); after timeout, engine auto-cascades with reason='hitl_timeout'.
acceptanceCriteria: Spec JSON supports `hitlPauseOnFailure: 'none' | 'terminal-only' | 'all-transient' | 'after-max-recovery'` (default 'after-max-recovery').
Spec JSON supports `hitlPauseTimeoutMinutes: number` (default 30, min 1, max 1440).
Migration (fresh timestamp) adds `pipeline_runs.paused_mode TEXT NULL` and `pipeline_runs.paused_reason TEXT NULL`. Allowed values for paused_mode: 'hitl_cascade_prevention', 'legacy_sigstop', NULL.

When HITL conditions are met at END OF WAVE (not per-failure), the engine collects ALL eligible blockers from this wave into a single pause event. It emits ONE `run_blocked` WAL event with `{ run_id, wave_index, reason: 'hitl_required', blockers: [{ storyId, failureReason, recoveryClass, recoveryAttempts, stderrTailSnippet }], deferredStoryIds: string[], resumeActions: ['context', 'resume', 'skip-story'], timeoutAt: ISO8601 }`.
The engine sets `pipeline_runs.status='paused'`, `paused_mode='hitl_cascade_prevention'`, `paused_reason='hitl_wave_${waveIndex}_blockers_${count}'` via SQL update.

Engine enters a poll loop: setInterval(3000ms) checks for three flag files in `<workspacePath>/forge/logs/`: `run-${runId}-context.txt` (context injection), `run-${runId}-resume.flag` (generic resume), `run-${runId}-skip-story-${storyId}.flag` (per-story skip). The engine process remains ALIVE — no SIGSTOP, no CPU spin (sleep between polls).
Engine also polls the DB every 10s for `pipeline_runs.status='cancelled'` — a cancel during HITL exits the poll loop cleanly.

New endpoint `POST /api/pipeline/runs/:runId/skip-story` body `{ storyId: string }` writes `run-${runId}-skip-story-${storyId}.flag` (JSON: `{ skippedAt: ISO, by: userId }`). Returns 200 on success, 404 if run not in paused state, 400 if storyId not in current blockers.

Existing `/context` endpoint's SIGCONT behavior is guarded: if `pipeline_runs.paused_mode='hitl_cascade_prevention'`, the endpoint ONLY writes the context file (the poll loop will pick it up); the SIGCONT send is SKIPPED. This requires a small edit to pipeline.ts line ~3504.

On context pickup: the engine reads the context file, deletes it, then for EACH blocker invokes dispatchRecovery() with the context appended to the story's recovery-context block. This gives one more recovery attempt per blocker WITH the operator's injected guidance.
On /resume pickup: engine deletes the flag, cascades all blockers as-is (no further recovery), resets pipeline_runs.status='running'.
On /skip-story pickup for storyId X: engine marks X as policy_fail, cascades X's subtree, but continues attempting recovery on OTHER blockers in the same pause event.

After timeout: engine emits `hitl_timeout` WAL event with `{ run_id, wave_index, timeout_minutes, blockers_abandoned: string[] }`, sets pipeline_runs.status='running', cascades all blockers, continues to next wave.

UI: Run View shows a prominent amber 'HITL Paused' banner when pipeline_runs.paused_mode='hitl_cascade_prevention', listing all blockers with expand-for-stderr and three action buttons (Inject Context modal, Retry As-Is, Skip Story dropdown).

Integration test 2: same scenario; test POSTs /context with `"the API schema is v2 now"` after 2s; engine picks up, appends to recovery context, attempts one more recovery per blocker; if stub succeeds, stories pass.
Integration test 3: same scenario; test POSTs /skip-story with one of the two blocker IDs; engine cascades ONLY that one's subtree; continues recovery on the other blocker.
Integration test 4: timeout — hitlPauseTimeoutMinutes=1 (1 min), engine pauses, no resume, after 60+3s engine emits hitl_timeout and cascades.
Integration test 5: cancellation during HITL — pipeline_runs.status set to 'cancelled' by external actor; poll loop exits within 10s; engine terminates gracefully without further cascade.

userStories.title: Observability: recovery metrics + FinOps panel
userStories.description: Operators need visibility into how recovery is affecting cost and reliability. Add metrics: (1) `recovery_successes` — count of stories that executed a recovery_attempt and eventually passed in the same run (measurable: a story with story_results.recovery_attempts >= 1 AND status='pass'); (2) `recovered_descendants` — count of stories that would have been cascade-blocked if ancestor failed but executed because ancestor recovered (measurable: stories with no blocked_by status in runs where at least one of their transitive ancestors has recovery_attempts >= 1 AND status='pass'); (3) `recovery_wasted_attempts` — count of recovery attempts that did not result in eventual pass (recovery_attempts > 0 AND status='fail'); (4) `recovery_wasted_tokens` / `recovery_wasted_dollars` — token/dollar cost of failed recovery attempts (joined with token_usage table); (5) `recovery_success_rate` — recovery_successes / (recovery_successes + stories_with_recovery_attempts_that_failed). These are OBSERVABLE metrics — no counterfactual required. Expose `GET /api/analytics/recovery` returning these aggregates with optional filters (workspaceId, dateRange, specId). Update Analytics panel with a Recovery card (4 KPI tiles + pie chart of recovery-by-reason + trend line over last 30 days).
acceptanceCriteria: New query function `getRecoveryStats(workspaceId?: string, dateRange?: {from: Date; to: Date}, specId?: string)` in backend/src/lib/analytics.ts returning the metric object.

Return shape: `{ totalRuns, runsWithRecovery, recoverySuccesses, recoveredDescendants, recoveryWastedAttempts, recoveryWastedTokens, recoveryWastedDollars, recoverySuccessRate, byReason: Record<string, { attempted: number, succeeded: number, failed: number }>, byStrategy: Record<RecoveryStrategy, { attempted, succeeded, failed, avgDurationMs }> }`.
`recoverySuccesses` SQL: `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT (run_id, story_id)) FROM story_results WHERE recovery_attempts >= 1 AND status = 'pass'`.

`recoveredDescendants` is computed by a WITH CTE: first identify recovered stories per run, then find stories whose dependsOn (read from spec JSON via helper) includes any recovered story, AND status='pass'. This requires reading spec JSON from `forge/specs/approved/<specPath>` — a cached resolver avoids redundant file reads.
`recoveryWastedAttempts` SQL: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM story_results WHERE recovery_attempts > 0 AND status = 'fail'` — these are attempts that failed anyway.
`recoveryWastedTokens` / `recoveryWastedDollars`: JOIN token_usage ON (run_id, story_id) for rows where recovery_attempts > 0 AND status='fail'. Sum input_tokens+output_tokens and cost_usd.
`recoverySuccessRate`: `recoverySuccesses / (recoverySuccesses + recoveryWastedAttempts)`. Returns 0 when denominator is 0.
`byReason` and `byStrategy` are built from `wal_events` JOIN `recovery_dispatch` / `story_recovery_*` events — pivot by payload->>'reason' and payload->>'strategy'.
New route `GET /api/analytics/recovery` with @swagger annotation. Query params: `workspaceId`, `from` (ISO date), `to` (ISO date), `specId`. Returns the shape above.

Analytics panel (src/panels/AnalyticsPanel.tsx) gains a 'Recovery' card with 4 KPI tiles: Recovery Successes, Recovered Descendants, Wasted Attempts, Success Rate. Plus a pie chart of byReason and a bar chart of byStrategy.
SSE-based live updates: subscribes to story_recovery_succeeded, story_recovery_failed, story_passed (with via='recovery') WAL events; updates KPIs within 3 seconds.
Empty state (0 runs with recovery): panel shows 'Cascade prevention is enabled but no failures have required recovery yet.' with docs link.
Docstring on getRecoveryStats explicitly defines each metric with its SQL and expected semantics.

userStories.title: Worker-side reconciliation: recover from engine crashes during in-run recovery
userStories.description: When the engine process is killed (SIGTERM from worker, OOM, host restart) during attemptBlockerRecovery(), the DB shows an incremented story_results.recovery_attempts but no terminal recovery WAL event (story_passed via='recovery' OR story_recovery_failed). The FailureRecord's `recoveryInFlight=true` exists only in engine memory and is lost on crash. Without reconciliation, orphaned in-flight recoveries either (a) block the next spawn of the engine because the DB state is inconsistent, or (b) get ignored and the story cascades permanently despite potentially being recoverable. This story adds worker-side reconciliation to detect and clean up these orphans. Runs whenever worker starts (recoverStaleJobs entry) and periodically (every 5 min) while worker is alive. Detection: query for runs in status='running' OR status='paused' where the engine process is dead (PID not alive) AND story_results has rows with recovery_attempts > 0 AND no corresponding terminal event (story_passed|story_recovery_failed) in wal_events within the last 10 minutes. Action: emit synthetic story_recovery_failed with reason='engine_crash_during_recovery', set pipeline_runs.status='failed' with failure_mode='recovery_orphaned'.
acceptanceCriteria: backend/src/worker.ts gains a new function `reconcileOrphanedRecoveries()` called from `recoverStaleJobs()` at worker startup AND from a setInterval(5 * 60 * 1000) periodic tick.

Detection SQL identifies (run_id, story_id) pairs where: pipeline_runs.status IN ('running', 'paused') AND (pipeline_runs.pid IS NULL OR pid is dead per isPidAlive()) AND story_results.recovery_attempts > 0 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM wal_events WHERE event_type IN ('story_passed','story_recovery_failed') AND payload->>'run_id' = pipeline_runs.id::text AND payload->>'story_id' = story_results.story_id AND ts > NOW() - INTERVAL '10 minutes').

For each detected orphan, insert a synthetic wal_events row: event_type='story_recovery_failed', payload includes `{ run_id, story_id, reason: 'engine_crash_during_recovery', recovered_by: 'worker_reconciliation', attempt: <current recovery_attempts value> }`.
For runs with orphaned recoveries, UPDATE pipeline_runs SET status='failed', failure_mode='recovery_orphaned', finished_at=NOW() WHERE id=<runId>.
A log line is emitted per reconciled orphan: `[worker] Reconciled orphaned recovery: run=<id>, story=<id>, reason=engine_crash_during_recovery`.
Reconciliation does NOT attempt to re-run the story — cross-run retry via /api/pipeline/runs/:id/retry is the user-controlled recovery path from this state.
A migration (fresh timestamp, format YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_pipeline_runs_failure_mode.sql) adds `failure_mode TEXT NULL` to pipeline_runs if not already present.

Integration test: spawn engine, simulate recovery-in-flight state (recovery_attempts=1, no terminal event), SIGKILL engine, run reconcileOrphanedRecoveries() — verify synthetic event is emitted and run.status='failed' with failure_mode='recovery_orphaned'.
Integration test: healthy in-flight recovery (live PID, heartbeat recent) is NOT reconciled (false-positive guard).
Integration test: old terminal event within 10 min window means orphan is NOT reconciled (the run was properly completed, just tagged late).
Reconciliation is idempotent — running it twice on the same orphan does not produce duplicate synthetic events (INSERT guarded by NOT EXISTS check).
The 10-minute window is a const `ORPHAN_DETECTION_WINDOW_MINUTES = 10` — can be tuned without code changes beyond that constant.

userStories.title: Partial-failure auto-merge: preserve passed-story commits when a run ends with some cascades
userStories.description: Under the classic engine, runs ended with exit=0 (all passed) or exit=1 (any failure). autoMergeRunWorktree (execution-engine.ts line 2437) runs only on exit=0. With cascade-prevention, 'partial_failure' becomes the common case: 27 of 30 stories passed, 3 cascaded. The 27 passed stories have commits on the run-level worktree branch (feat/<slug>-<ts>) but auto-merge never fires, leaving the branch unmerged and operators confused. This story: (1) introduces `partial_failure` as an explicit pipeline_runs.status value alongside 'done' and 'failed'; (2) engine exits with code 2 for partial_failure (vs 0 for all-pass, 1 for all-fail/pre-wave-failure); (3) worker handles exit 2 by setting status='partial_failure'; (4) autoMergeRunWorktree is invoked for BOTH exit 0 and exit 2 — passing commits merge to main with a merge message that calls out the cascaded stories; (5) a new spec-level toggle `partialFailureAutoMerge: boolean` (default true) can disable this per-spec for conservative operators. The merge commit message: 'merge: <branchName> (partial — N/M stories passed, cascaded: [S1, S2, S3])'.
acceptanceCriteria: execution-engine.ts main() exit codes are updated: `process.exit(0)` when all stories passed; `process.exit(2)` when at least one story passed AND at least one failed/cascaded; `process.exit(1)` when no stories passed (catastrophic failure, pre-wave error, or worktree creation fully failed).

Migration (fresh timestamp) adds the CHECK constraint: `CHECK (status IN ('queued','running','paused','done','failed','cancelled','partial_failure'))`. Existing rows are NOT affected since existing values are all still allowed.
backend/src/worker.ts's job completion handler maps exit code 2 → status='partial_failure'. Exit code 0 → 'done'. Exit code 1 → 'failed'. Other → 'failed'.
autoMergeRunWorktree() is invoked for both exit 0 AND exit 2 (partial_failure). Exit 1 leaves the branch alone for manual inspection.
The merge commit message for partial_failure: `merge: ${branchName} (partial — ${passedCount}/${totalCount} stories passed, cascaded: ${cascadedStoryIds.join(', ')})`. For full success, unchanged.
Spec JSON supports top-level `partialFailureAutoMerge: boolean` (default true). If false, partial_failure runs skip the auto-merge.
If merge fails for a partial_failure run (conflicts with main), the branch is preserved for operator inspection (same graceful degradation as existing autoMergeRunWorktree).

userStories.title: Concurrency-safety audit: catalog all shared state touched by recovery + wave+1 execution
userStories.description: CP-003 establishes serialization (wave N's recovery completes before wave N+1 starts). But multiple implicit shared-state hazards remain. This story is an explicit audit + fix pass. Catalog every piece of state that the recovery phase and the next wave's execution could both touch: (a) `config.cwd` HEAD (git ref) — recovery's mergeStoryWorktree moves it; next wave's createStoryWorktree branches off it. CP-006 uses a captured SHA to avoid the race but this story verifies it's the ONLY place. (b) `retryCounts` Map — recovery deletes entries; next wave's stories may share entries by storyId collision? Verify no collision possible since storyIds are unique per spec. (c) `failureRegistry` Map — recovery mutates; next wave reads. Must be mutex-free because single-threaded JS runtime guarantees atomicity of Map ops, BUT async boundaries matter. (d) spec JSON file on disk — recovery writes markStoryPassed; next wave reads via JSON.parse. File is read inside wave loop at line 4060 (getStories(JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(...)))) — verify this happens AFTER recovery completes. (e) run-state.json — recovery writes (rsMarkStoryPassed); next wave reads. Atomic write already enforced by existing code. (f) Git worktree directory `.git/worktrees/<spec>-<story>` — recovery creates recovery worktrees; next wave creates original worktrees. Naming collision impossible due to recovery suffix, but verify. Output: each identified shared-state item gets an explicit AC — either 'already safe' with reasoning, or 'needs fix' with the fix implemented.
acceptanceCriteria: A checklist document at `docs/cascade-prevention-concurrency-audit.md` lists all shared-state items between recovery phase and next-wave execution, each with one of: SAFE (with reasoning), FIXED (with commit SHA linking to the fix), or KNOWN-LIMITATION (with operational mitigation).
`config.cwd` HEAD: SAFE because CP-003 enforces serialization (recovery awaited) and CP-006 captures a concrete SHA for rebase target (not a moving ref).
`retryCounts` Map: SAFE because storyIds are globally unique per spec (compileWaves throws on collision) and recovery only mutates its own storyId entry.
`failureRegistry` Map: SAFE because JS single-threaded runtime guarantees atomic Map ops; CP-003 serialization ensures no cross-wave race.

Spec JSON file: VERIFIED — the reread at line 4060 (`allStories = getStories(JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(config.jsonPath, 'utf8')))`) happens AFTER attemptBlockerRecovery's awaited return. Add a regression test that proves this ordering.
run-state.json: SAFE — rsMarkStoryPassed uses atomic rename-based writes (verify by reading run-state.ts implementation; document the guarantee).
Git worktree directories: SAFE — recovery worktrees have `recovery-N` suffix AND optional UUID collision-breaker; next wave's worktrees use original naming. Cross-phase collision impossible.

A new integration test `concurrency-audit.test.ts` exercises each item above with a scenario that WOULD FAIL if the safety assumption were wrong (e.g. mutate the spec JSON during recovery, verify next wave reads the updated state).
If any item is flagged as 'needs fix' during the audit, the fix is implemented in this same story (no follow-up story required).
A new section in CLAUDE.md (under Cascade Prevention) titled 'Concurrency Safety' links to the audit doc and summarizes the guarantees.

Worker-side concurrency: verify that the worker's heartbeat writer (every 60s) and the engine's in-process writes to pipeline_runs don't race on the same row. Use pg row-level locking or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE only if a race is observed (document whether needed).
